When more regulatory T cells do not mean better control

Bang et al. Allergology International. 2026;75(3):488-499.

Methods in this study
  • 39-parameter CyTOF
  • viSNE / FlowSOM
  • Public PBMC and skin scRNA-seq reanalysis
  • Treg suppression assay
  • Tissue immunofluorescence

01 / The question

The question

Do expanded regulatory T cells in atopic dermatitis retain effective suppression, or do they contain distinct functional states?

02 / How we tested it

How we tested it

PBMCs from 48 people with AD and 48 controls were profiled using 39-parameter CyTOF and clustering. Reanalysis of public PBMC and skin scRNA-seq was combined with in vitro OX40⁺ Treg suppression assays and tissue immunofluorescence.

How the evidence connects

CyTOF, functional assays and skin immunofluorescence were performed in this collaborative study; scRNA-seq evidence came from public-data reanalysis. Functional assays involved 5 HC and 3 AD donors, and skin immunofluorescence involved 7 participants per group.

03 / What the study found

What the study found

A Treg population with high OX40 and CRTH2 expression was associated with disease severity. OX40⁺ Tregs from AD donors showed lower suppressive capacity than the corresponding OX40⁺ population from controls, with enrichment also supported in skin.

04 / Interpreting the evidence

Interpreting the evidence

The main cohort was Korean and the functional assays involved few donors. In vitro findings do not fully reproduce the skin microenvironment, and the study does not establish prediction of responses to OX40-targeted treatment.

Figures from the paper

Complete Figure 6a–f: complementary evidence from public skin scRNA-seq and tissue immunofluorescence. CyTOF and suppression assays are not shown in this figure.

The next question

A question to explore together

Could longitudinal sampling of skin and blood reveal how changes in OX40⁺ Treg states relate to clinical response?
